# Exodus 25 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

Exodus 25 opens the third major section of the book (chapters 25–40), which concerns the tabernacle and its worship. God gives Moses instructions while he is still on Mount Sinai. J. Sidlow Baxter notes that Scripture devotes more room to the tabernacle than to any other single subject, and seven times the charge is repeated to make everything according to the “pattern” shown on the mountain (Ex 25:9, 40; 26:30; 27:8; Num 8:4; Acts 7:44; Heb 8:5). (preceptaustin.org)

---

### v. 1 — “Then the LORD said to Moses…”

**God’s direct speech begins.** Moses is still on Mount Sinai, and the instructions for the tabernacle will continue through the end of Exodus 31. The HCSB Study Bible notes that the phrase “The LORD spoke to Moses” divides Exodus 25–31 into seven unequal segments, ending with the Sabbath command — creating a parallel with the seven days of creation. (preceptaustin.org)

---

### v. 2 — “Tell the Israelites to bring Me an offering … from every man whose heart compels him.”

**Voluntary, heart-driven giving.** God asks for an offering *before* specifying what it is for. David Guzik (Enduring Word) writes: “God wanted Israel to be motivated by a willing heart more than by a specific need … Our giving should not be primarily because of need. We should primarily give because our willing heart compels us.” (enduringword.com)

Ellicott notes the Hebrew reads “every man whose heart impels him,” adding: “Unless gifts come from the heart, they are an offence to God. He ‘loveth a cheerful giver.’” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

Gill observes that the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan call this offering a “separation” — something separated from one’s substance and devoted to God. He also notes Jewish tradition excluded Gentiles, minors, deaf-mutes, and fools because “they have no knowledge to offer freely.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)

Precept Austin notes the Hebrew word for “contribution” (*teruwmah*) is translated in the Septuagint as *aparche*, meaning “first-fruits.” The contribution was a “heave offering” — something lifted up toward heaven. (preceptaustin.org)

The Pulpit Commentary homiletics section stresses: “The value of beautiful forms is a thing only too easily exaggerated. But no one can exaggerate the beauty of a spiritual action, the beauty of a gift where the willingness and devotion of the whole heart are manifest.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics)

**Reformed connection:** Guzik ties willing giving to sanctification: “When we become givers, we become more like God, who is the greatest giver: ‘For God so loved the world, He gave His only begotten Son’ (John 3:16).” The same principle is echoed by Paul in 2 Corinthians 9:7. (enduringword.com)

---

### v. 3 — “gold, silver, and bronze”

**Metals in descending value.** Gold was the most costly, bronze the least. Precept Austin cites Currid: “In the tabernacle, the closer an object was to the Holy of Holies, the more valuable was the metal used in its construction.” This principle — the closer to God’s presence, the more precious the material — governs the entire tabernacle design. (preceptaustin.org)

Ellicott notes the Israelites’ wealth came from their ancestral possessions, the gifts from Egyptians at the Exodus, and plunder from the Amalekites. The bronze (*nechosheth*) was actually copper alloyed with tin — true brass was unknown at this time. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

---

### v. 4 — “blue, purple, and scarlet yarn; fine linen and goat hair”

**Dyed yarns and fabrics for curtains and priestly garments.** Ellicott explains: blue dye came from indigo (the only blue known to Egypt); purple came from the *murex trunculus* shellfish (the famed “Tyrian purple”); scarlet came from the *coccus ilicis* insect (a cochineal-like bug of the holm oak). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

Enduring Word adds: fine linen translates an Egyptian word — Egypt excelled in linen production. Goat hair was coarse and black, similar to modern felt, and was used for the tent’s outer covering, just as Bedouin tents are made of goat hair to this day. (enduringword.com)

Precept Austin notes the list runs from most costly (dyed fabrics) to least costly (goat hair). Fine linen is associated with meeting God in the sanctuary, and in Revelation 19:7–8 it represents “the righteous acts of the saints” at the marriage supper of the Lamb. (preceptaustin.org)

---

### v. 5 — “ram skins dyed red and fine leather; acacia wood”

**Ram skins dyed red:** Ellicott observes that North Africa has always been famous for fine leather production, and brilliant red was a favoured colour. Israelites likely brought these from Egypt. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

**Fine leather (badger skins):** The Hebrew *takhash* is uncertain. Ellicott says “badger” is an improbable translation since the badger is not native to North Africa or Arabia. The Arabic *tukhash/dukhash* refers to a marine animal like a seal, dugong, or dolphin. These skins formed the outermost covering of the tabernacle (Ex 26:14). Enduring Word similarly notes it may refer to porpoise or manatee skins. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

**Acacia wood:** Ellicott identifies this as *Acacia Seyal*, a “gnarled and thorny tree” native to the Sinai region. The wood is hard, close-grained, orange-coloured, and avoided by wood-eating insects. Clarke notes it was plentiful in Egypt and Arabia Deserta — exactly where Moses was building. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

---

### v. 6 — “olive oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense”

Ellicott notes it is already assumed the sanctuary will need light, so oil must be provided. Later (Ex 27:20) it is specified that the oil must be “pure olive oil beaten.” The spices for anointing oil are enumerated later in Exodus 30:23–24, and those for incense in Exodus 30:34. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

---

### v. 7 — “onyx stones and gemstones to be mounted on the ephod and breastpiece”

Ellicott notes the Hebrew *shoham* is uncertain — the LXX renders it “sard,” the Vulgate “sardonyx,” Rosenmüller “beryl,” and Job 28:16 in the LXX calls it “onyx.” Only three such stones were needed as offerings: one for the high priest’s breastpiece and two for the ephod’s shoulder-pieces. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

---

### vv. 8–9 — “And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them. You must make the tabernacle … according to the pattern I show you.”

**v. 8 — Purpose: God dwelling among His people.** The Hebrew for “sanctuary” (*miqdash*) means a holy place set apart for Jehovah. “Dwell” (*shakan*) conveys the idea of temporary lodging in a tent, fitting the nomadic lifestyle. In the Septuagint, *shakan* is translated with the passive of *horao* — “to become visible,” emphasising that God will not only dwell there but be visibly present, likely in the Shekinah glory cloud. (preceptaustin.org)

Ellicott expands: Israel had had no dedicated place of worship until now. Having seen the vast Egyptian temples, they were now to have their own “holy place.” Because they were nomadic, God devised a “tent-temple” — modelled on fine Oriental tents, portable yet magnificent. God’s dwelling was not purely spiritual; He manifested Himself sensibly in the Holy of Holies. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that God required the materials from the people rather than supplying them miraculously: “These people who had required so many interventions of God to deliver and secure them had yet been carrying with them … the great store of wealth indicated in this passage.” God takes our treasures — things that seemed useless in the wilderness — and consecrates them. (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics)

**v. 9 — The heavenly pattern.** Cole says the word “pattern” means “almost ‘architect’s model.’” The tabernacle was “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Heb 8:5). Ellicott says three views exist: (1) a material model was shown; (2) a pictorial representation; (3) a series of visions — and “the entire analogy of the Divine dealings is in favour of the last-mentioned view.” (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

Guzik notes the tabernacle was a *tent*, not a permanent building, so that Israel would understand God as “a fellow-pilgrim” who pitched where they pitched — “their enemies, difficulties, and long toilsome marches were His” (Meyer). (enduringword.com)

---

### v. 10 — “an ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high”

**The most important item.** The ark is described first because it was “the symbol of the approach to God” (Thomas), modelled after God’s throne in heaven. Constable calls it “the throne of Yahweh where He dwelt in a localized way … the seat of His sovereignty but also the place where He met with His people.” The dimensions: approximately 3 ft 9 in × 2 ft 3 in × 2 ft 3 in. (enduringword.com; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

The Hebrew word *aron* (chest/coffer) is different from the word for Noah’s ark (*tebah*). It was a chest — not a boat. Ellicott notes that sacred coffers were common in Egyptian temples, usually containing an image or emblem of a deity. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott; preceptaustin.org)

---

### v. 11 — “Overlay it with pure gold both inside and out, and make a gold molding around it”

Ellicott says this was likely done with gold plates, not gilding — gold plate was more valuable and more suited to desert conditions. The “molding” (or “crown”) was a rim around the top edge, probably to hold the mercy seat in place. The gold overlay inside and out speaks of the holiness and glory of God’s presence — nothing base was to be seen. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott; enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 12–15 — Rings and poles for carrying

**v. 12:** Four gold rings were cast and fastened at the “four feet” — the bottom corners (not the top). Ellicott explains this was so the ark, when carried on priests’ shoulders, would be elevated above them, preventing contact with the bearers. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

**v. 13–14:** Poles of acacia wood overlaid with gold were inserted through the rings. The ark was never to be lifted directly by human hands — only carried via the poles.

**v. 15 — “The poles are to remain in the rings of the ark; they must not be removed.”** Guzik emphasises the gravity of this command: when Uzzah later touched the ark directly (2 Sam 6:6–7), even with good intentions, he violated this command and died instantly. “Uzzah was wrong in his thinking that God would let the Ark be damaged … Uzzah was also wrong in his thinking that there was something less pure about the ground than his act of pure disobedience.” Ellicott adds: the staves remained always in the rings “that there might never at any time be a necessity for touching the ark itself, or even the rings. He who touched the ark imperilled his life.” (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

---

### v. 16 — “And place inside the ark the Testimony, which I will give you”

“The Testimony” = the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments. Ellicott says they were called “the Testimony” as “God’s witness against sin” (Deut 31:26). Constable: “God’s dwelling among His people and His relationship with them thus quite literally rested on the Ten Commandments.” Later, a jar of manna and Aaron’s budding rod were also placed inside (Heb 9:4), though by Solomon’s time only the tablets remained (1 Kgs 8:9). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc; enduringword.com)

Guzik notes: “God told Moses to build the Ark of the Covenant to hold the law even before the law was given.” (enduringword.com)

---

### vv. 17–22 — The Mercy Seat and the Cherubim

**v. 17 — “a mercy seat of pure gold, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide.”** The mercy seat (*kapporeth*) was the solid gold lid of the ark, matching its dimensions exactly. Ellicott insists the translation “mercy seat” (LXX: *hilasterion*; Vulgate: *propitiatorium*) is correct against critics who translate it merely as “lid” or “cover.” He argues that *kapporeth* derives from *kipper* (“to expiate sins”), not *kaphar* (“to cover”). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

Kaiser translates *kapporeth* as “atonement cover.” Guzik notes: “The ark was the place of atonement or propitiation, hence the place where God was rendered favorable to his people.” (enduringword.com)

**The Reformed/Ligonier connection:** Ligonier’s article “What Is the Mercy Seat?” highlights that the Septuagint translates *kapporeth* as *hilasterion* — the same Greek word Paul uses for Christ in Romans 3:25: “God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement [*hilasterion*].” Ligonier states: “God desires to meet with His people, and the blood of the spotless lamb is the only means … The mercy seat of the Old Testament, and the blood sprinkled upon it by the high priest, prefigured Christ to come.” Constable makes the same link to 1 John 2:2. (learn.ligonier.org; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

**v. 18–20 — Two cherubim of hammered gold.** Made from the same piece of gold as the mercy seat (not attached separately), the cherubim faced each other with wings spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat, their faces gazing downward toward it. Ellicott says the cherubim were “the guardians of Eden” (Gen 3:24) — a select class of powerful angels near to God. The predominant opinion among commentators (Kalisch, Keil, Bishop Harold Browne, Canon Cook) is that they had human form with wings, resembling the Egyptian figures of Ma (Truth) that sheltered sacred emblems inside Egyptian arks. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

Cole notes that cherubim were “God’s attendant and messenger spirits” and their manufacture “was not considered a breach of Exodus 20:4, since no man worshipped them.” Constable adds they “symbolized angelic guardians of the invisible throne of God.” (enduringword.com; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

**v. 21 — “Set the mercy seat atop the ark, and put the Testimony … into the ark.”** The arrangement: law inside the ark, blood-sprinkled mercy seat above it.

**v. 22 — “And I will meet with you there above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim … I will speak with you about all that I command you regarding the Israelites.”** Guzik paints the picture: “It was as if God, looking down from His dwelling place between the cherubim, saw the law in the Ark — and knew we were guilty of breaking His law. But atoning blood of sacrifice was sprinkled on the mercy seat, so that God saw the blood covering the breaking of His law — and forgiveness could be offered.” He adds the remarkable observation: “even before God gave Moses the tablets of the Ten Commandments, God made provision for Israel’s failure under the law.” (enduringword.com)

Ellicott calls this “the place of the Shechinah, or visible manifestation of God’s presence.” God would meet His people there — either literally (Urim and Thummim) or spiritually (accepting incense, blood, and prayers). The entire tabernacle was therefore called “the Tent of Meeting.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

---

### vv. 23–30 — The Table of Showbread

**v. 23–24 — “a table of acacia wood two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. Overlay it with pure gold and make a gold molding around it.”** Dimensions: approximately 3 ft × 1.5 ft × 2 ft 3 in. Like the ark, it was acacia wood overlaid with gold plates. The “molding” (or “crown”) was an ornamental edging. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

**v. 25 — “a rim around it a handbreadth wide and put a gold molding on the rim.”** Ellicott interprets this as a “band or framing” — a flat bar about midway between the tabletop and the feet, connecting the four legs. The Arch of Titus in Rome shows this table being carried away as spoil, confirming its design. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott; enduringword.com)

**v. 26–28 — Rings and poles.** Four gold rings at the four feet, with acacia-overlaid-gold poles — the same carrying method as the ark, though the table was less sacred.

**v. 29 — Plates, dishes, pitchers, and bowls of pure gold.** Ellicott explains: “dishes” were large bowls for bringing loaves to the table; “spoons” (*kaph*) were small pots for burning incense (Lev 24:7); “covers” and “bowls” were flagons and chalices for drink offerings. The Arch of Titus shows two such incense pots on the table. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

**v. 30 — “And place the Bread of the Presence on the table before Me at all times.”** “Bread of the Presence” (*lechem panim*) literally means “bread of faces” — either because it was placed before the face of God, or, as some Jewish tradition holds, because the loaves were square. Twelve loaves (one per tribe) were arranged in two rows, sprinkled with frankincense, replaced every Sabbath, and normally eaten only by priests (Lev 24:5–9). (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)

Guzik: “In the East a table was always the symbol of fellowship. Thus the people were reminded of the possibility created of constant communion with God” (Morgan). Constable: the bread was “a perpetual thank offering to God from the twelve tribes for the blessings that they received from Him day by day.” (enduringword.com; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

**Reformed view (Monergism):** The bread reminded Israel of God’s covenant — just as the elders ate a meal in God’s presence to ratify the covenant (Ex 24:11), the priests eating the bread recalled Israel’s redemption and God’s provision. The bread also finds New Testament connections in Christ’s feeding of the five thousand, the Lord’s Supper, and the Lord’s Prayer (“give us this day our daily bread”). (monergism.com)

---

### vv. 31–40 — The Golden Lampstand (Menorah)

**v. 31 — “a lampstand of pure, hammered gold … made of one piece, including its base and shaft, its cups, and its buds and petals.”** No dimensions are given, but it followed the pattern of what we now call a menorah. It was hammered (*not* cast) from a single piece of gold. Constable notes the lampstand stood opposite the table of showbread on the south side of the holy place. (enduringword.com; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

**v. 32–36 — Six branches (three per side) plus the central shaft = seven lamps.** The decorative motif was almond blossoms with buds and petals. Guzik explains the almond tree was “the first tree to blossom in the springtime,” symbolising “new life and the fresh nature of God’s ongoing work.” The buds under each pair of branches emphasised unity — “all of one piece.” (enduringword.com)

Constable quotes Keil and Delitzsch at length: the almond tree derives its Hebrew name (*shaqed*) from being the earliest to blossom and fruit (cf. Jer 1:11–12). The almond blossom represented “the seasonable offering of the flowers and fruits of the Spirit.” The lampstand’s seven arms bore “the stamp of the covenant relationship.” (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

**v. 37 — “Make seven lamps and set them up … so that they illuminate the area in front of it.”** Since the tabernacle was a completely covered tent, the lampstand was the *only* source of light inside. Guzik connects the seven lamps to Revelation 4:5 — “seven lamps of fire were burning before the throne, which are the seven Spirits of God” — representing the Holy Spirit’s presence in heaven. (enduringword.com)

Cole offers a complementary view: “The symbolism might be that of the light which God’s presence brings to His people (Num 6:25), remembering that light, in the Old Testament, is also a symbol of life and victory (Psalm 27:1).” (enduringword.com)

Constable adds: the lampstand “symbolized Yahweh’s Presence in perpetual wakefulness, through the reminder of the almond tree and the continual brightness of the living fire … The watcher over Israel never nodded, much less slept (Psalm 121:4)” (Durham). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

**v. 38–39 — Wick trimmers, trays, all pure gold; a talent of gold total.** Kaiser says a talent was about 75 pounds (34 kg) of gold — a massive investment. The wick trimmers and trays (for spent wicks) were also pure gold — even the humblest utensils were precious. (enduringword.com)

**v. 40 — “See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.”** This repeats the principle from v. 9. Constable notes the order of description in these chapters is significant: God is described *from the inside out* — first the ark in the Holy of Holies, then the table and lampstand in the holy place, then the courtyard. The focus is on God’s presence at the centre of His people, with materials decreasing in value (gold → silver → bronze) radiating outward from the centre. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

Precept Austin notes this phrase is one of seven such commands in Scripture (Ex 25:9, 40; 26:30; 27:8; Num 8:4; Acts 7:44; Heb 8:5), and Hebrews 8:5 explicitly ties the earthly tabernacle to the heavenly reality: “They serve at a sanctuary that is a copy and shadow of what is in heaven.” (preceptaustin.org)

---

## Points Where Traditions Differ or Add Distinctive Emphases

### The Mercy Seat and Atonement Theology

- **Reformed (Ligonier/Constable):** Strong emphasis on the mercy seat as *hilasterion* (propitiation) — the place where God’s wrath is satisfied. Christ is the ultimate mercy seat (Rom 3:25). The blood on the mercy seat appeased God’s wrath, prefiguring Christ’s substitutionary atonement. (learn.ligonier.org; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Emphasises the personal communion aspect — God meeting and speaking with His people. The seven lamps represent the Holy Spirit (Rev 4:5), and the lampstand’s almond blossoms speak of new life and fresh anointing. The tabernacle as a whole is about God dwelling *with* His people as a fellow-pilgrim. (enduringword.com)

### The Bread of the Presence

- **Reformed (Monergism):** Sees the bread primarily as a covenant meal — recalling the meal the elders ate before God (Ex 24:11) and pointing forward to the Lord’s Supper. The table is about God’s provision and the covenant relationship. (monergism.com)

- **Broader Evangelical (Constable/Guzik):** Emphasises the bread as representing the twelve tribes in constant communion with God, a thank offering for daily provision. Constable suggests the bread may also symbolise “Israel’s vocation” — Israel was to be a source of spiritual food for the world (Ex 19:5–6). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

### Typological Interpretation: How Much Is “Too Much”?

Constable raises an important caution: not every detail of the tabernacle is necessarily a “type” of Christ. A “type” is a *divinely intended* illustration; the New Testament explicitly identifies only certain things as types (Adam, the wilderness wanderings, the holy place, the flood). He writes: “I prefer a cautious approach … it seems to me that there are many illustrations of New Testament truth in the Old Testament.” He contrasts this with commentators who assign symbolic meaning to every colour, number, and material — and with Josephus, who (following Philo) interpreted the seven lamps as the seven planets, the colours as the four elements, and the twelve stones as the zodiac. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc)

---

## Other Views

### Catholic/Orthodox

No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary pages for Exodus 25 were found within the permitted sources. However, the Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org) and Orthodox Church in America (oca.org) sites would generally affirm the traditional typological reading: the ark prefigures Mary as the “Ark of the New Covenant” (bearing Christ, the Word made flesh), and the tabernacle foreshadows the Incarnation (John 1:14: “the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us”). This Marian typology is distinctive to Catholic and Orthodox interpretation but was not obtained from the searched sources.

### Modern Scholarship / NET Bible Notes

The NET Bible note on the ark (cited at preceptaustin.org) states: “The point of this item in the tabernacle is to underscore the focus: the covenant people must always have God’s holy standard before them as they draw near to worship. A study of this would focus on God’s nature (he is a God of order, precision, and perfection), on the usefulness of this item for worship, and on the typology intended.” (preceptaustin.org)

*Sources used: enduringword.com, preceptaustin.org, studylight.org (Constable), biblehub.com (Ellicott, Gill, Pulpit), gotquestions.org, learn.ligonier.org (search excerpt), monergism.com.*
